definition.text: The interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals.

facts.text: It covers exposure to or deficiency of trace elements and minerals, mineral dusts, volcanic emissions, radionuclides, microbes and pathogens.
Its two stated priorities are the bioavailability of trace elements and baseline background levels of harmful natural materials in soil, water, air and food.
People who live off the land face either impoverished soils that cause mineral-imbalance diseases, as in Maputaland, or an excess of elements causing toxicity, as in India and Bangladesh.
Iodine deficiency is one of the biggest geochemical diseases; humus and clay in soil trap iodine and make it hard for people to obtain.
Regional problems include fluoride in Africa and India, arsenic in Argentina, Chile and Taiwan, selenium in parts of the US, Venezuela and China, and nitrate in farm areas.
Paracelsus's dictum that the dose makes the poison sums up the field, whose goal is the right balance of element intake.
Hippocrates and Aristotle first linked disease to the earth's elements; the modern field was established in 1990 by the International Union of Geological Sciences.

definition.text: The deliberate eating of earth or earth-like substances such as clay, chalk or termite-mound soil, by animals and people.

facts.text: It is documented in over 100 primate species, where it protects against parasites, supplies minerals and helps neutralize toxic compounds in leaves.
In humans it is most often reported in children and pregnant women and is classed as a form of pica.
The oldest evidence comes from Kalambo Falls, where calcium-rich white clay lay alongside Homo habilis bones.
Kaolin is sold for eating in Cameroon markets and eaten by pregnant women against nausea, despite possibly dangerous arsenic and lead levels.
Clay minerals may protect the stomach against toxins, parasites and pathogens, and many soils supply calcium, iron and zinc.
Faecally contaminated soil can pass on helminth eggs such as Ascaris, which survive in soil for years, as well as tetanus and lead poisoning.
Bentonite and kaolin are sold as digestive aids, and attapulgite clay is an active ingredient in anti-diarrhoeal medicines.

definition.text: The eating of clay-rich soil by birds, notably South American parrots at clay licks.

facts.text: Parrots on the Manu River eat from one specific soil layer, ignoring layers a metre above or below it.
Preferred soils are rich in smectite, kaolin and mica and have far higher cation-exchange capacity, so they bind toxins from seeds that become positively charged in the stomach.
Consumed soils are consistently higher in sodium, and geophagy increases with distance from the ocean, making sodium the likely main driver.

definition.text: The swallowing of soil by grazing animals such as cattle and sheep, pressed onto pasture plants by their hooves.

facts.text: It is measured from the ash content of faeces and is greatest on weak, poorly drained soils in wet autumn and winter conditions.
Soil supplies grazers with iron, manganese, zinc, cobalt, copper, selenium and iodine that herbage lacks, but can wear down sheep's incisors.

definition.text: A disease of the lymphatic vessels of the lower legs, also called nonfilarial elephantiasis, caused by long-term barefoot contact with irritant soils.

facts.text: It is the second most common cause of tropical lymphoedema after lymphatic filariasis, causing disfiguring leg swelling.
It occurs in genetically susceptible people in contact with red clay soils formed over alkaline volcanic bedrock in highlands with about 1500 mm of rain at 1500 m altitude.
Affected areas are enriched in kaolinite and gibbsite; smectite, mica, quartz and iron oxides are also suspects, but no single culprit is proven.
Soil particles penetrate the feet, are taken up by macrophages and collect in lymph nodes, causing chronic inflammation, fibrosis and blockage.
Ernest Price showed silicon, aluminium and other soil metals inside macrophages in patients' lymph nodes.
An estimated 4 million people are affected, 1.5 million in Ethiopia; wearing shoes and using floor coverings prevent it.

definition.text: Infection with roundworms spread through soil contaminated with human faeces: ascariasis, hookworm and whipworm.

facts.text: It is the most common human parasitic disease, with about two billion people infected and four billion at risk.
Eggs passed in faeces mature into infective larvae in soil and are swallowed on unwashed produce or hands; hookworm larvae instead hatch and penetrate the skin.
Its main causes are open defecation, lack of hand washing and walking barefoot on contaminated soil, so it is commonest in warm, moist, poorly sanitized regions.
Hookworm is the leading cause of anaemia and protein deficiency in developing nations, affecting an estimated 740 million people.
Deworming reduces worm burdens, but reinfection follows continued exposure; improved water, sanitation and hygiene lower the odds of infection.

definition.text: Valley fever: a fungal disease of mammals caused by inhaling spores of the soil fungi Coccidioides immitis or C. posadasii.

facts.text: The fungus grows as a mycelium in soils of the southwestern US, northern Mexico and parts of Central and South America.
Rain starts its growth; in long dry spells its hyphae break into light arthroconidia that construction, farming, dust storms or earthquakes lift into the air.
A 1977 windstorm near Arvin, California, caused several hundred cases hundreds of miles from the endemic area.
Incidence rises after wet winters that follow drought, and one model projects the endemic region could more than double in area by 2100 under high warming.
Dust control such as planting grass and wetting soil is advised, and NIOSH counts it an occupational hazard in farming, construction, archaeology and mining.
Dogs, which dig and sniff at the ground, are exposed earlier than people and serve as sentinels.

title: Melioidosis

definition.text: An infectious disease caused by the soil-dwelling bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, caught by contact with contaminated soil or water.

facts.text: The bacterium is most abundant 10 to 90 cm deep in soil and also lives in ponds, streams and rice paddies.
It survives more than 16 years in nutrient-poor settings such as desert soil, and tolerates pH 4.5 for 70 days.
It enters through wounds, inhalation or ingestion; it is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and cases rise with heavy rain and storms.
A 2016 model estimated about 165,000 infections and 89,000 deaths a year; diabetes is a major risk factor.
Latent infections earned it the name 'Vietnam Time Bomb' after soldiers fell ill years after deployment.
Prevention includes protective gear for handling soil or water and avoiding direct contact with them; there is no approved vaccine.

notes: Also draws on the Burkholderia pseudomallei page (the causative organism), folded in here rather than given its own entry.

definition.text: A lack of the essential dietary trace element iodine, which the thyroid hormones need.

facts.text: It is common in remote inland and especially mountainous areas, where food grows in iodine-poor soil and no marine foods are eaten.
It causes goitre, and in the womb a syndrome of developmental delay; it is a preventable cause of intellectual disability.
Natural deficiency affects about two billion people, particularly in the Western Pacific, South-East Asia and Africa; goitre affected 187 million in 2010.
Adding small amounts of iodine to table salt, at a cost of only a few cents a ton, is the main prevention.
Selenium deficiency is among its risk factors.

definition.text: A shortage of selenium, a critical nutrient, below the levels an organism requires.

facts.text: People who depend on food grown in selenium-deficient soil are at risk.
Croplands and diets are low in selenium in regions of China, Europe, Russia and New Zealand, and loss of selenium from croplands under climate change is predicted to raise prevalence.
Combined with Coxsackievirus it causes Keshan disease, and with iodine deficiency it contributes to Kashin-Beck disease of cartilage.
Finland adds selenium salts to chemical fertilizers to raise soil selenium.
In livestock it causes white muscle disease, to which ruminants are especially prone because they absorb less selenium, particularly from forage.
Adult intake recommendations are 55 μg/day in the US and 70 μg/day from the European Food Safety Authority.

definition.text: A congestive cardiomyopathy caused by dietary selenium deficiency together with a mutated strain of Coxsackievirus, named after Keshan County in China.

facts.text: It was found across a belt from northeast to southwest China, all due to selenium-deficient soil, and peaked in 1960–1970, killing thousands.
Selenium deficiency appears to let a more virulent viral strain dominate.
Selenium supplementation over decades reduced it, and some patients use Astragalus, a herb that accumulates selenium from soil.
Vegetables such as garlic, onions and broccoli are good selenium sources only if their soil contains it.

definition.text: The mass cadmium poisoning in Toyama Prefecture, Japan, from about 1912, named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused.

facts.text: Mines upstream released cadmium into the Jinzū River from 1910 to 1945; cadmium accompanies zinc because the ore sphalerite is almost always paired with greenockite.
Residents irrigated rice with the river water; the highly soluble cadmium contaminated paddies and rice, raising body burdens.
Cadmium accumulated in the kidneys, and kidney damage disrupted calcium balance, causing the bone pain and deformities.
Cadmium was suspected only in 1955, and the 1961 investigation tied it to the Kamioka mine, 55 years after the first reports.
It is one of the Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan, and the mining company was successfully sued.

definition.text: The cleanup of cadmium-polluted farmland along Japan's Jinzū River after the itai-itai disease lawsuit.

facts.text: Japan's 1970 agricultural soil contamination law stopped planting for restoration where soil held 1 ppm cadmium or more; by 1977, 1,500 hectares were designated.
By 2012, 863 hectares of topsoil had been replaced since 1979 at a cost of ¥40.7 billion.
By 1996 cadmium in the farmland had returned to a background level of 0.1 ppb.

definition.text: Breeding crops, conventionally or by genetic engineering, so that they contain more nutrients as they grow.

facts.text: It targets micronutrient deficiencies such as vitamin A, zinc and iron in low- and middle-income countries, reaching the rural poor who rarely get fortified foods.
Beta-carotene sweet potatoes cut vitamin A deficiency in Mozambican children by 24%, and iron- and zinc-rich pearl millet improved iron status in India.
Researchers are developing bread grain biofortified with selenium to raise low selenium levels in British grains.
Critics warn it may further simplify diets and urge it be part of wider food diversification.

title: Hygiene hypothesis

definition.text: The idea that early-childhood exposure to certain microorganisms protects against allergies by properly tuning the immune system.

facts.text: Later versions, such as Graham Rook's 2003 'old friends' hypothesis, focus on microbes that co-evolved with humans rather than recent crowd infections.
Rook's candidates include ambient species sharing human environments, and most mammalian evolution took place in mud and rotting vegetation.
Much evidence supports it, yet many scientists still reject it, and it struggles to explain allergies in less affluent regions.
It is not about personal cleanliness: poor hygiene raises infection risk without lowering allergy risk.

contested_note: The sources say the hypothesis has substantial support but is still rejected by many scientists.

definition.text: A nonpathogenic bacterium of the Mycobacteriaceae that lives naturally in soil.

facts.text: It was first isolated in Uganda, where locals said a muddy substance could cure ailments; its name comes from cow dung, where the first strain was cultured.
Heat-killed cells injected into mice raised serotonin and lowered anxiety, and mice fed live cells ran a maze twice as fast with less anxiety.
Killed-cell vaccines are being studied for asthma, depression, psoriasis, eczema and tuberculosis.

definition.text: An integrated approach that seeks to balance and optimize the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together.

facts.text: It arose from the spread of zoonotic diseases and awareness that human and animal health and ecological change are interdependent.
Antimicrobial resistance is treated as a One Health issue: misuse in medicine, veterinary care and farming selects resistant organisms, and wastewater, soil and runoff spread them.
It is backed by the FAO, WHO, the World Organisation for Animal Health and UNEP.

definition.text: A misfolded protein that makes normal copies of the same protein misfold, causing fatal, transmissible neurodegenerative diseases.

facts.text: Prions contain no DNA or RNA and cause diseases such as scrapie, chronic wasting disease, BSE and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease.
Shed from carcasses and body fluids, they may linger in soil by binding to clay and other minerals.

Unbound prions degrade over time, but soil-bound ones stay stable or increase, so prions likely accumulate in the environment; repeated wetting and drying may reduce their infectivity, depending on soil type.
Hamsters fed grass grown where a deer with chronic wasting disease was buried became ill, showing plants can carry prions.

definition.text: A fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathy caused by prions that naturally affects deer, elk, moose and their relatives.

facts.text: Prions shed by infected animals are transmitted by eating grass growing in contaminated soil, and stay infectious in the environment for years.
They bind so tightly to soil particles that the ground may be a major route of transmission for grazing deer.
Prions mixed with clay infected deer through the nose, and they were shown by 2006 to bind to sandy quartz clay minerals.
After a Quebec outbreak, inspectors ordered 25 cm of soil decontaminated in parts of the farm.
